guideTitle: 6 Best Video Intercom Systems Under $300 in 2026
metaDescription: Compare six video intercom kits with touchscreens, 1080P cameras and multi-monitor layouts, plus advice on which household each one fits best.
introParagraphs: Moving up a tier in video intercoms mostly buys you three things: sharper cameras, touchscreen monitors, and extra indoor screens. Cheaper kits tend to give you a single press-key monitor and a basic camera, while this group starts to offer 1080P video, phone apps and two-wire retrofit options.

We evaluated each system from its listing and specs, comparing monitor count, camera resolution, wiring style and unlock features. Because this page leans toward the stronger half of the price range, several picks here add touch controls or phone alerts that you will not find on the most basic sets.

The best fit depends on your building more than the feature list. A house that already has doorbell wire wants a different kit than a three-flat building that needs a screen per household, so use the pick notes and the decision tables to match the kit to the door.

products.name: LUMOBELL 2-Wire Dual 7-Inch Touch Intercom
products.description:
LUMOBELL targets homeowners who already have a doorbell wire in place. Its two-wire design can reuse that existing wiring, which keeps a retrofit from turning into a renovation, and the kit includes two 7-inch touchscreen monitors. The doorbell camera records in 1080P, and you can see visitors on the monitor or through your phone.

The listing also describes motion-detection alerts that send phone notifications when something moves near the door, plus a door-release function. Touch panels feel more modern than press keys, though they make the monitor a little more sensitive to fingerprints and cleaning. The listing does not make clear every accessory in the box, so verify the contents before buying.

Once installed, it behaves like a smart doorbell with indoor displays, which is a different experience from the older AMOCAM kits here. It is better suited to a single home than the AMOCAM 3-Unit set, and its two monitors match the KeonBell touch kit on screen count while using a thinner cable run.
products.bestFor: A single home with existing doorbell wire that wants two touch screens and phone alerts.
pros: Reuses existing doorbell wiring for retrofits
Two 7-inch touch screens for different rooms
1080P camera with phone viewing option
Motion alerts reach your phone
cons: Touch panels show fingerprints more than keys
Accessory list needs checking before buying

products.name: AMOCAM 3-Unit Wired Apartment Intercom
products.description:
This is a conventional multi-unit kit: one outdoor camera with infrared night vision serves three households, and each household gets a 7-inch LCD monitor. Residents can answer, monitor and unlock with press keys, and there is a mute option plus 16 chime tones. Volume, brightness and contrast are all adjustable on the screen.

Its value comes from sharing one camera and one entry panel across three homes instead of buying three separate doorbells. The cabling is traditional multi-wire, so each monitor needs a run back to the central connection, and press keys feel dated next to a touch interface. Shared-entry kits also need a clear agreement on who pays for and maintains the unit.

Against the AMOCAM Upgraded 3-Unit set it covers the same number of homes without the ethernet and keyfob features, so it is the simpler choice if your cabling is already planned. Compared with the LUMOBELL it is more of a building solution than a single-home upgrade.
products.bestFor: Three flats sharing one street door that want a straightforward wired setup.
pros: One outdoor camera serves three households
Each flat gets its own 7-inch monitor
Infrared night vision on the entry camera
Mute option and adjustable screen settings
cons: Press keys feel dated beside touch controls
Multi-wire cabling needs planning for each flat

products.name: AMOCAM Upgraded 3-Household Ethernet Intercom
products.description:
The upgraded AMOCAM set swaps the old multi-wire approach for network cable. The outdoor camera and each monitor use a network interface, and only the camera needs to be plugged in for power. It supports three households from one entry, and the package includes five ID keyfobs.

A keyfob lets residents open the door without picking up the monitor, which matters in a shared hallway where people carry shopping or hold a child. The door lock can be opened in two ways, and the keyfob set includes one to add and one to delete cards. The price of that convenience is cable: every household needs an ethernet run to the camera.

In practice, this is the pick for a building where a tidy cabling plan is realistic, such as a new build or a refurbishment with open walls. The plain AMOCAM 3-Unit kit is easier to install but has no keyfob access. The LUMOBELL is a better match for a single house than this shared-entry design.
products.bestFor: A three-household building that wants tap-in keyfob access and tidier cabling.
pros: Keyfobs let residents enter without answering
Network cable layout is neat and testable
Only the camera needs mains power
Three monitors for three separate homes
cons: Needs ethernet runs to every household
Too complex for a simple single door

products.name: KeonBell 2-Wire 1080P Two-Monitor Intercom
products.description:
KeonBell offers one camera and two 7-inch touchscreen monitors on a two-wire connection, with night vision and remote unlock. The listing describes notifications through the Tuya app so you are told when a visitor rings, plus the ability to see and talk from a phone. You can also forward a call between monitors and use the intercom function to talk room to room.

The call transfer and indoor intercom are useful in a bigger house, where you might want to ask someone upstairs to answer. The trade is that the two-wire build makes this a one-door system, not a multi-household one. As with other budget sets, check the exact included parts on the listing.

Setup mirrors the LUMOBELL, using a thin pair of conductors, but the KeonBell adds call forwarding that the LUMOBELL does not describe. It beats the Tmezon on cable simplicity because that kit uses four wires. If you want an app and touch screens without paying for a wider system, it is a balanced choice.
products.bestFor: A two-floor house that wants touch screens, call forwarding and phone alerts.
pros: Call transfer between the two monitors
Room-to-room intercom talk between screens
Tuya app notifications on visitor rings
Thin two-wire run simplifies retrofits
cons: Single-door system, not built for flats

products.name: AMOCAM Wired 7-Inch 800x480 Camera Kit
products.description:
The monitor here is the story: a 7-inch LCD at 800 x 480, which is a defined resolution rather than a vague claim. The outdoor camera has a 92-degree angle, infrared night vision and a waterproofed aluminum and acrylic front panel meant to withstand vandalism. It also includes 16 chime tones with adjustable volume, brightness and contrast.

That build suits a door that takes weather, such as a gated entry or an open porch. The camera angle is narrower than a 1080P wide-angle doorbell, and the interface is press-key, not touch. The listing leaves its accessories to be confirmed, so check for lock cables and mounting hardware.

It is a single-door system, so it does not cover multiple flats the way the AMOCAM 3-Unit kit does. Against the LUMOBELL and KeonBell you give up 1080P video and touch screens in exchange for a tougher outdoor panel. It makes sense when the physical durability of the camera matters more than app features.
products.bestFor: An exposed gate or porch that needs a durable camera and a clear screen.
pros: Defined 800 x 480 resolution on the monitor
Aluminum and acrylic panel resists vandalism
Infrared night vision on the outdoor camera
Adjustable brightness and contrast on screen
cons: Press-key controls, no touch or app features

products.name: TMEZON Ring-Style 1-Camera 2-Monitor System
products.description:
TMEZON packages a ring-style camera with two 7-inch indoor monitors and a four-wire connection. The camera has infrared night vision, and the system supports two-way intercom plus remote unlock through a gate-lock output. Screen volume, brightness and contrast are adjustable, with 16 chime tones.

The marketing points it at larger single-family properties, which makes sense because two monitors let you place screens far apart. The compromise is a four-wire install, which takes more care than a two-wire kit, and there is no app listed. Double-check the box contents on the listing, as with the other kits.

Compared with the KeonBell it has no touch interface or phone alerts, but its familiar layout is easy for an electrician to wire. Against the AMOCAM 3-Unit kit it serves one home with two screens instead of three homes with one each. It is the most traditional kit here, and that can be a plus for buyers who prefer simplicity.
products.bestFor: A larger single-family home that wants two wired screens and no app dependence.
pros: Two monitors placed far apart in a big home
Gate-lock output supports remote unlock
No app or WiFi needed to function
Infrared camera for evening visitors
cons: No touch screen or phone features listed

buyingCriteria.explanation: Touch panels such as those on the LUMOBELL 2-Wire Dual 7-Inch Touch kit and the KeonBell 2-Wire 1080P kit feel closer to a smartphone and make menus quicker to navigate. Press keys, as on the AMOCAM 3-Unit and TMEZON kits, are tactile and hard to misread. If the monitor will be used by older relatives or in a busy kitchen, press keys are often easier. If you want call forwarding and settings menus, touch is the better fit.

A higher-resolution camera helps you recognise a face or read a delivery label. The LUMOBELL and KeonBell list 1080P cameras, while the AMOCAM 800 x 480 kit lists a screen resolution of that size. Look for 1080P if you expect to check the picture on a phone, since small screens hide fine detail. For a quick glance at a 7-inch monitor, the gap is smaller than the spec sheet suggests.

Two-wire kits like the LUMOBELL and KeonBell reuse thin cable, which suits retrofits. Four-wire kits like the TMEZON need more conductors, and the AMOCAM Upgraded 3-Household set uses ethernet cable. Count the run length from the door to each screen before buying. A long cable path in an older home is often the biggest hidden cost.

Some kits at this level add a phone layer. The LUMOBELL lists motion alerts and phone viewing, and the KeonBell lists Tuya app notifications. Traditional wired sets like the AMOCAM 3-Unit and TMEZON skip this. Choose an app only if you will use it, because a phone link adds a WiFi dependency and an account to manage.

Match the screen count to the people, not to the feature list. The AMOCAM 3-Unit and AMOCAM Upgraded sets give each of three households a monitor, while the KeonBell and TMEZON kits give one home two. A shared entry also benefits from keyfobs, as the Upgraded kit supplies five. Adding a monitor later is usually harder than buying the right count first.

The outdoor unit takes rain, sun and knocks. The AMOCAM 800 x 480 kit lists an aluminum and acrylic front panel with waterproofing and a 92-degree angle. Doorbell-style cameras such as the LUMOBELL and KeonBell look neater but may be less rugged. Shield the camera under an eave if your listing does not describe a robust housing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Interface and usability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how each kit is operated day to day, from touch panels to press keys. The LUMOBELL and KeonBell lead on modern touch interfaces, while the AMOCAM and TMEZON kits keep simple buttons. We also checked whether call forwarding or intercom features were described.

howWeEvaluated.title: Camera quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the resolution and viewing angle on each listing. The LUMOBELL and KeonBell list 1080P, and the AMOCAM 800 x 480 kit lists a 92-degree lens. We treated night vision as essential and weighed the lens angle against how wide a typical entry is.

howWeEvaluated.title: Installation and wiring
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged how much cabling each kit demands, since wiring is the main cost of ownership. Two-wire designs scored best for retrofit, while the AMOCAM Upgraded ethernet kit scored lower on simplicity but higher on tidiness. Based on specs and buyer feedback, we flagged where a listing was vague.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage for the household
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how many homes or rooms each system serves. The AMOCAM 3-Unit and Upgraded kits serve three households, the KeonBell and TMEZON serve one home with two screens, and the LUMOBELL does the same with touch. The lineup divides cleanly into building kits and house kits.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at this budget
howWeEvaluated.description: We asked whether each kit's extras justify its place in the upper half of the range, and what a buyer would need to spend beyond it. Keyfobs, app alerts and 1080P counted as meaningful upgrades. Pure chime melodies counted for little.

cards.label: Two-wire systems
cards.text: A pair of conductors carries power, video and audio, so the LUMOBELL and KeonBell kits can reuse an old doorbell run. The limit is expansion and compatibility. Choose these if you have a single door and want minimal cable.

cards.label: Multi-wire and ethernet
cards.text: The TMEZON, AMOCAM 3-Unit and AMOCAM 800x480 kits use more conductors, and the AMOCAM Upgraded uses ethernet cable. These setups take more planning, but they scale to multiple monitors or households. Choose them when you are cabling a new or open space.

faq.q: Which kit suits a house with an old doorbell wire?
faq.a: The LUMOBELL 2-Wire kit is built to reuse existing doorbell wiring. The KeonBell is also two-wire, so either avoids a big cable job. Check that your existing wire is in good condition before relying on it.

faq.q: Is 1080P worth it on a 7-inch monitor?
faq.a: On the monitor alone the jump is modest, but it matters if you watch through a phone. The LUMOBELL and KeonBell list 1080P for that reason. If you will only glance at the screen, a lower-resolution camera still shows who is there.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two AMOCAM three-household kits?
faq.a: The AMOCAM 3-Unit set uses conventional wiring and press keys, while the Upgraded set uses ethernet and adds five ID keyfobs. The Upgraded one is tidier but needs network cable runs. Choose the simpler one if you already have wire in place.

faq.q: Can I answer from my phone?
faq.a: Only the kits with an app, such as the LUMOBELL and KeonBell, are described that way. The TMEZON and AMOCAM sets are closed monitors. If remote answering matters, confirm the app details and any account needs.

faq.q: Do these systems replace a lock?
faq.a: No. They release an existing electric lock or gate motor, so you still need a compatible lock. Check the voltage and type before you buy, and ask an electrician if you are unsure whether your strike is fail-safe or fail-secure. A mismatch is the most common reason a new intercom talks fine but never opens the door.

faq.q: How long should a wired kit last?
faq.a: Indoor screens usually outlast the outdoor camera because the camera faces weather. The AMOCAM 800x480 kit has the sturdiest panel on this list. A sheltered position and sealed cable joins extend life.

faq.q: Is a shared-entry kit hard to maintain?
faq.a: It is simple day to day, but agree on who handles repairs. Keyfobs on the AMOCAM Upgraded set can be added or removed, which helps when residents change. Keep a spare fob and note the cable layout. A short written guide taped inside the cabinet saves a lot of guesswork the next time someone moves in or out.
